'''Eva Nogales''' (born May 16, 1965)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://colmenarviejo.com/comunicacion/noticias/colmenar-viejo-entrega-la-medalla-de-hija-predilecta-a-evangelina-nogales-de-la-morena|title=Colmenar Viejo entrega la medalla de Hija Predilecta a Evangelina Nogales de la Morena — Ayuntamiento de Colmenar Viejo}}</ref> is a Spanish-American [[biophysicist]] at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] and a professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where she served as head of the Division of Biochemistry, Biophysics and Structural Biology of the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology (2015–2020). She is a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator.

Nogales is a pioneer in using [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]] for the structural and functional characterization of macromolecular complexes. She used [[electron crystallography]] to obtain the first structure of [[tubulin]] and identify the binding site of the important anti-cancer drug [[Paclitaxel|taxol]].{{cn|date=June 2026}} She is a involved in work combining [[Transmission electron cryomicroscopy|cryo-EM]], computational image analysis and [[Assay|biochemical assays]] to gain insights into function and regulation of biological complexes and [[molecular machine]]s.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.mdtmag.com/news/2016/12/how-see-living-machines|title=How to See Living Machines|date=December 7, 2016|work=Medical Design Technology|access-date=February 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180204124042/https://www.mdtmag.com/news/2016/12/how-see-living-machines |archive-date=February 4, 2018}}</ref> Her work has uncovered aspects of cellular function that are relevant to the treatment of cancer and other diseases.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/eva-nogales|title=Eva Nogales|website=HHMI.org|language=en|access-date=March 23, 2019}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Eva Nogales obtained her BS degree in physics from the [[Autonomous University of Madrid]] in 1988.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Nogales Lab – CryoEM – Publications |url=http://cryoem.berkeley.edu/eva.html |access-date=March 16, 2022 |website=cryoem.berkeley.edu |archive-date=December 25, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211225201816/http://cryoem.berkeley.edu/eva.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> She later earned her PhD from the [[University of Keele]] in 1992 while working at the [[Synchrotron Radiation Source]] under the supervision of [[Joan Bordas]].<ref name=":0" />

==Career==
During her post-doctoral work in the laboratory of Ken Downing at  the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], Eva Nogales was the first to determine the atomic structure of [[tubulin]] and the location of the taxol-binding site by [[electron crystallography]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nogales|first1=E.|last2=Wolf|first2=S. G.|last3=Khan|first3=I. A.|last4=Ludueña|first4=R. F.|last5=Downing|first5=K. H.|date=June 1, 1995|title=Structure of tubulin at 6.5 A and location of the taxol-binding site|journal=Nature|volume=375|issue=6530|pages=424–427|doi=10.1038/375424a0|issn=0028-0836|pmid=7760939|bibcode=1995Natur.375..424N|s2cid=4338992}}</ref><ref>Nogales, E., Wolf, S. G. and Downing, K. H. (1998.) Structure of the ab tubulin dimer by electron crystallography. ''Nature'', 391, 199-203.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nogales|first1=E.|last2=Whittaker|first2=M.|last3=Milligan|first3=R. A.|last4=Downing|first4=K. H.|date=January 8, 1999|title=High-resolution model of the microtubule|journal=Cell|volume=96|issue=1|pages=79–88|issn=0092-8674|pmid=9989499|doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(00)80961-7|s2cid=18422680|doi-access=free}}</ref>  She became an assistant professor in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1998. In 2000 she became an investigator in the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]. As [[Transmission electron cryomicroscopy|cryo-EM]] techniques became more powerful,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Callaway|first=Ewen|date=September 10, 2015|title=The revolution will not be crystallized: a new method sweeps through structural biology|journal=Nature|volume=525|issue=7568|pages=172–174|doi=10.1038/525172a|issn=1476-4687|pmid=26354465|bibcode=2015Natur.525..172C|doi-access=free}}</ref> she became a leader in applying cryo-EM to the study of microtubule structure and function<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Downing|first1=Kenneth H.|last2=Nogales|first2=Eva|chapter=Cryoelectron Microscopy Applications in the Study of Tubulin Structure, Microtubule Architecture, Dynamics and Assemblies, and Interaction of Microtubules with Motors |date=2010|title=Cryo-EM, Part C: Analyses, Interpretation, and Case studies|series=Methods in Enzymology|volume=483|pages=121–142|doi=10.1016/S0076-6879(10)83006-X|issn=1557-7988|pmc=4165512|pmid=20888472|isbn=9780123849939}}</ref> and other large [[macromolecular assemblies]] such as [[eukaryotic transcription]] and translation initiation complexes,<ref>Michael A. Cianfrocco, George A. Kassavetis, Patricia Grob, Jie Fang, Tamar Juven-Gershon, James T. Kadonaga, Eva Nogales (2013.) Human TFIID Binds to Core Promoter DNA in a Reorganized Structural State. ''Cell'', 152(1):120–131.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genengnews.com/news/stop-motion-view-of-dna-binding-complex-may-animate-drug-discovery/|title=Stop-Motion View of DNA-Binding Complex May Animate Drug Discovery|date=November 20, 2018|website=GEN – Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News|language=en-US|access-date=March 23, 2019}}</ref> the polycomb complex PRC2, and [[telomerase]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.technologynetworks.com/drug-discovery/articles/the-3d-structure-of-telomerase-uncovering-its-role-in-human-disease-300278|title=The 3D Structure of Telomerase: Uncovering Its Role in Human Disease|website=Drug Discovery from Technology Networks|language=en|access-date=March 23, 2019}}</ref>

* 2015: Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin Award, [[Protein Society]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2015-02/tps-atw020415.php|title=Announcing the winners of the 2015 Protein Society Awards|website=EurekAlert!|language=en|access-date=March 23, 2019}}</ref>
* 2015: Elected as a member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]]<ref name="nasonline.org 2021 r165">{{cite web | title=Eva Nogales | website=nasonline.org | date=April 16, 2021 | url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/eva-nogales-vxz44a/ | access-date=December 29, 2023}}</ref>
* 2016: Elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.dailycal.org/2016/04/22/9-campus-faculty-selected-membership-american-academy-arts-sciences/|title=9 campus faculty selected for membership in American Academy of Arts and Sciences {{!}} The Daily Californian|date=April 22, 2016|work=The Daily Californian|access-date=February 3, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref>

* 2019: Grimwade Medal for Biochemistry.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://biosciences.lbl.gov/2019/03/07/nogales-receives-2019-grimwade-medal/|title=Nogales Receives 2019 Grimwade Medal|date=March 7, 2019|website=Biosciences Area|language=en-US|access-date=March 23, 2019}}</ref>
* 2021: [[AAAS Fellow]]s Award.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AAAS Honors Outstanding Scientific Contributors as 2021 AAAS Fellows {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-honors-outstanding-scientific-contributors-2021-aaas-fellows |access-date=March 16, 2022 |website=www.aaas.org |language=en}}</ref>

* 2025: Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 20, 2025 |title=Exceptional scientists elected as Fellows of the Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2025/05/new-fellows/ |access-date=May 22, 2025 |website=Royal Society |language=en}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Nogales is married to Howard Padmore and they have two children.<ref name="Phelan 2014 q953">{{cite web | last=Phelan | first=Laura | title=Eva Nogales | website=The [[Biophysical Society]] | date=December 1, 2014 | url=https://www.biophysics.org/membership-communities/representation-and-access/biophysicists-in-profile-dei/eva-nogales | access-date=September 7, 2026}}</ref>
